title: Children, Slaves, Masters, and the Armor of God
summary: Paul completes the household instructions: children are to obey their parents, and fathers are not to provoke their children but raise them in the Lord's discipline; slaves are to serve sincerely as to Christ, and masters are to stop threatening them, knowing they share the same Master in heaven who shows no favoritism. He then calls all believers to be strong in the Lord and put on the full armor of God to stand against the devil's schemes, and to pray at all times. The letter closes with news of Tychicus and a blessing of peace and grace.
story: The household instructions that began at 5:21 with mutual submission continue here, moving from marriage to the other two pairs of the ancient household. Then, with the word finally (v. 10), Paul widens the frame. The struggles of home and work, and the whole life of the church described in chapters 4 and 5, take place within a larger conflict with spiritual powers. The letter began with Christ seated above every rule and authority (1:20-21); it ends with believers standing firm against those same powers in God's strength. The closing verses return to Paul's own situation as an ambassador in chains and send the letter on its way with Tychicus.
historical:
Slavery was woven into every part of the Roman world. Slaves worked in households, fields, mines, workshops, and civic offices; some were educated managers or teachers, others labored in brutal conditions. People became slaves through capture in war, birth to enslaved mothers, debt, abandonment as infants, or sale. Roman slavery was not based on race, and many urban slaves could hope to be freed, but a slave was legally property: he or she could be bought, sold, beaten, separated from family, and used sexually by the master. Many early Christians were slaves, and some were masters, and both belonged to the same congregations.

Tychicus (v. 21) was from the province of Asia and traveled with Paul (Acts 20:4). Colossians 4:7-9 describes him carrying that letter together with Onesimus, a runaway slave returning to his master Philemon. The overlap of names and wording suggests Ephesians and Colossians were sent at the same time.
cultural:
Children in the Roman household were under the father's legal authority for as long as he lived, and harsh discipline was common. Paul's command that fathers not provoke their children to wrath (v. 4) placed a limit on paternal power that ordinary household codes did not. The quotation of the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16) grounds the children's duty in Israel's law and its promise.

The armor in verses 14 to 17 resembles that of a Roman soldier, which Paul, chained to guards, may have seen daily: belt, breastplate, sandals or boots, a large shield, a helmet, and a short sword. But the pieces come mainly from Isaiah, where God himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet (Isaiah 59:17), the Messiah wears righteousness and faithfulness as a belt (Isaiah 11:5), and beautiful feet bring good news of peace (Isaiah 52:7). The armor Paul describes is God's own armor, given to his people.
literary: Verses 1 to 9 keep the pattern of 5:22-33: each pair is addressed in turn, the one under authority first, and every instruction is tied to the Lord. The repetition is striking: obey in the Lord, as to Christ, as servants of Christ, as to the Lord, because the Lord will reward, their Master and yours is in heaven. Verses 10 to 20 are an extended metaphor in which each piece of armor names a gift of God: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God. The command to stand appears four times (vv. 11, 13, 14). Only the sword is used to strike; the rest is defensive, since the victory has already been won by Christ. Prayer (vv. 18-20) completes the passage rather than being one more piece of armor. The closing (vv. 21-24) is brief and general, with no personal greetings, which fits the view that the letter circulated among several churches.

outline.t: Slaves and masters under one Master
Be strong in the Lord: the struggle against the powers
Pray at all times; pray for Paul

doctrines.note: Children are addressed as members of the church who honor their parents in the Lord, and fathers are forbidden to rule by provocation. Parenting is framed as bringing children up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord, not as the exercise of power.

Every earthly master stands under the one Master in heaven, who shows no favoritism (v. 9). Paul places the most unequal relationship of his world under the judgment of a Lord who does not rank people by status.

The armor of God is made of what God gives in salvation: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation itself, and the word of God. Believers stand not in their own strength but in his mighty power (v. 10).
Prayer in the Spirit at all times is the context in which the armor is worn (v. 18). Paul, a prisoner, asks not for release but for boldness to proclaim the gospel.

words.note: Doulos, slave. English versions sometimes translate it servant, but in this setting it means a person owned by another. The same word describes believers as slaves of Christ (v. 6). Paul uses that double sense to tell slaves their true Master is Christ, and to tell masters that they have the same Master, before whom there is no favoritism.

Panoplia, full armor, the complete equipment of a heavily armed soldier; it gives English the word panoply. It appears twice (vv. 11, 13). The emphasis is on completeness: believers need every part of what God provides, not a selection.

Pale, struggle or wrestling. The word came from the wrestling of Greek athletics, a close, hand-to-hand contest. Paul says the believer's real struggle is not against flesh and blood, that is, against human enemies, but against spiritual forces of evil.

Paideia, discipline or training, the whole upbringing of a child, including instruction and correction. Fathers are to raise children in the discipline of the Lord (v. 4), training that belongs to him and reflects his character.

christ: Christ stands over every relationship in this chapter. Children obey in the Lord; slaves serve as to Christ; masters answer to the Master in heaven. The authority of Christ does not leave earthly hierarchies untouched: it relativizes them, since every person, slave or free, will receive from the Lord for whatever good he does (v. 8). In the second half of the chapter believers are strong in the Lord and in his mighty power, the same power that raised Christ and seated him above every authority (1:19-21). Isaiah pictured God and his Messiah putting on armor to bring justice and salvation; Paul says that armor now clothes Christ's people. Paul himself is an ambassador in chains for the mystery of the gospel, representing a king whose rule is not yet visible to the world.

hard.q: Why does Paul tell slaves to obey their masters instead of condemning slavery, and how have these verses been used?
hard.a:
Paul does not call for the abolition of slavery here, and readers should not soften that fact. He addresses a small, vulnerable movement inside an empire where slavery was assumed everywhere and slave revolts were crushed with great violence. Within that world he does several things that ordinary household codes did not: he speaks to slaves as moral persons and full members of the church; he tells masters to give up threats; he says masters and slaves have the same Master in heaven, who shows no favoritism; and elsewhere he tells slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21) and urges Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). Many interpreters see here the seeds of principles that undermine slavery itself: every person bears God's image, and in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28).

The history of these verses is painful. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used Ephesians 6:5 and similar texts to demand obedience from enslaved Africans and to defend slavery as biblical, while ignoring the commands to masters and the equality of all in Christ. An 1807 selection of Bible passages prepared for enslaved people in the British West Indies kept such texts while leaving out most of the story of Israel's release from slavery in Exodus. Christian abolitionists, on the other hand, drew on the Bible's teaching about human dignity, the exodus, and the gospel to oppose slavery. Modern slavery, built on race and kidnapping, differed in important ways from the Roman institution, but Paul's words were wrongly made to serve it. Reading this passage honestly means naming that misuse as sin and hearing the text as Paul framed it: a word that places every master under judgment.

questions: Paul tells fathers not to provoke their children to wrath. What provokes children, and what does bringing them up in the Lord look like in practice?
How does knowing that every employer, manager, and worker answers to the same Master change the way you approach your work?
Paul says our struggle is not against flesh and blood. How might that change the way you see the people you find hardest to love?
